paper.title: The Intergenerational Effects of Intermarriage
paper.journal: Journal of International Migration and Integration
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement is given, and no Statistics Denmark project number is reported. …

registers.name_in_paper: administrative registers, covering the full population of Denmark
registers.role: outcomes / treatment / controls / linkage / sample frame
variables_mentioned: final grades from nationally centralized class 9 final examinations in Danish and mathematics

parental labour-market status (unemployed vs employed or self-employed), 'based on information about personal income, education, industry of employment, unemployment insurance information, and reports from private companies'

registers.name_in_paper: nationally centralized final examinations in class 9 (grade records, 2002-2011)
variables_mentioned: grade average of the several exams taken in Danish
grade average of the several exams taken in mathematics

linkages: Families are linked across generations in the register data
Children linked to both parents (country of birth, highest education, labour-market attachment, separation)
Children linked to cousins through grandparents: 'For an individual to appear in the cousin sample, both grandparents and at least one cousin born to an aunt or uncle must be found in the data'
Students linked to schools, allowing school fixed effects (1963 schools in the Danish full sample, 1959 in the mathematics sample)

sample.universe: All students taking the nationally centralized class 9 final examinations in Danish and in mathematics in Denmark in the years 2002-2011, classified as native Danes, 2.5 generation (children of intermarriage) or second-generation immigrants.
sample.unit_of_observation: Student (cross-sectional: 'the data analyzed in this paper is cross-sectional since students take their class 9 exam once').
selection_rules: Student sat the class 9 nationally centralized final examination in the subject in 2002-2011
Student is born in Denmark and classified by parental origin as native Dane, 2.5 generation or second generation
Children of single parents are not included in the analysis
Cousin sample only: both grandparents and at least one cousin born to an aunt or uncle must be found in the data
Region-of-origin (Table 6) and parental-gender (Table 7) models: second-generation immigrants are excluded
sample.n_observations: 326,176 (Danish, full sample); 325,368 (mathematics, full sample); 104,344 (Danish, cousin sample, OLS); 102,202 in 49,444 families (cousin FE, native-Dane comparison); 12,669 in 9,332 families (cousin FE, second-generation comparison)
sample.n_individuals: One observation per student, so observations equal students; Table 1 reports 44,383 2.5 generation, 259,536 native Danes and 22,257 second generation in the Danish full sample, and Table 2 reports 10,408, 91,794 and 2142 respectively in the cousin sample

construction_notes: 'In order to ease the comparison, grades are standardized to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one within each school year.'
'In both subjects, several exams are taken, and the outcome variable is the grade average of several exams.'
Parental education is the highest education obtained by each parent at the time of the child's exam, in four categories: unknown, primary, secondary, tertiary
Parental labour-market attachment is a dummy: (0) unemployed and (1) employed or self-employed, created with the Employment Classification Module (AKM)
Models further control for parental separation, number of siblings, birth order and year

Parental region of origin is used as a proxy for country of origin; seven regions (Nordic, Western, Eastern Europe, Latin America, Africa, Asia, Middle East and Pakistan), country lists in Appendix Table 8

Native Danes are 'Born in Denmark with both parents born in Denmark'; second generation are 'Born in the receiving country with both parents born abroad'; the 2.5 generation have one native-born and one foreign-born parent
In the cousin sample about 10% of students belong to the 2.5 generation and about 2.5% are second-generation immigrants

claims.statement: Students classified as Native Danes differ from the 2.5 generation (children of intermarriage) in standardized class 9 Danish grades, in the crude OLS without covariates of Table 3, column (A) OLS.

treatment.label: Native Danes (student-group indicator; reference category: the 2.5 generation)

definition.value: Indicator for a native Dane, defined as 'Born in Denmark with both parents born in Denmark'. Estimated relative to the omitted category, the 2.5 generation, i.e. children of intermarriage born in Denmark with one native-born and one foreign-born parent.

timing.value: Parental country of birth, fixed at the child's birth; the group indicator is measured in the cross-section of the child's class 9 examination year.

outcome.label: Standardized grade average in Danish, class 9 nationally centralized final examinations

definition.value: Grade average of the several exams taken in the subject at the nationally centralized class 9 final examination; 'grades are standardized to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one within each school year'. Cross-sectional: students take their class 9 exam once.

timing.value: Measured once, at the student's class 9 nationally centralized final examination, in the examination years 2002-2011.

units.value: standard deviations of the within-school-year grade distribution (grades standardized to mean 0 and SD 1 within each school year)

estimand.target_population: Students who sat the class 9 nationally centralized final examination in Danish in Denmark between 2002 and 2011 and belong to the 2.5 generation, the native-Dane group or the second generation.

population.description: All students taking the class 9 nationally centralized final examination in Danish in Denmark, 2002-2011, classified as native Danes, 2.5 generation or second generation; children of single parents excluded.
population.selection: Students who sat the class 9 nationally centralized final examination in the subject in Denmark 2002-2011. 'Children of single parents are not included in the analysis.'

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation in parental nativity between students (and, in the fixed-effects columns, within schools or within extended families). No reform, lottery or discontinuity is used: 'the paper is mainly descriptive'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unobservable characteristics at the family level - values, upbringing practices and attitudes - are shared by intermarried and endogamously married parents and affect their children's school achievement; the author states these may bias the parameters and are not removed in this specification.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues that brothers and sisters are more likely to share these features than two random individuals and introduces cousin fixed effects to control for them partially; no test is offered.

evidence.how: The paper prints no mean of the standardized grade average for the reference group or for any student group: Tables 1 and 2 report only covariate means (parental education, birth region, separation, sex, year) and no grade means, and the table notes give none.
The outcome is standardized to SD one within each school year, so the SD of the outcome in the pooled estimation sample is 1 by construction; the paper prints no sample SD.

The paper names no register or register variable for grades or for parental country of birth: it says only that 'The analysis is based on administrative registers, covering the full population of Denmark'. The one register named anywhere is the Employment Classification Module (AKM), used for parental labour-market attachment.
The tables print standard errors in parentheses and significance stars; no confidence intervals are reported.

treatment.label: Native Danes (student-group indicator; reference category: the 2.5 generation)

definition.value: Indicator for a native Dane, defined as 'Born in Denmark with both parents born in Denmark'. Estimated relative to the omitted category, the 2.5 generation, i.e. children of intermarriage born in Denmark with one native-born and one foreign-born parent.

timing.value: Parental country of birth, fixed at the child's birth; the group indicator is measured in the cross-section of the child's class 9 examination year.

outcome.label: Standardized grade average in mathematics, class 9 nationally centralized final examinations

definition.value: Grade average of the several exams taken in the subject at the nationally centralized class 9 final examination; 'grades are standardized to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one within each school year'. Cross-sectional: students take their class 9 exam once.

timing.value: Measured once, at the student's class 9 nationally centralized final examination, in the examination years 2002-2011.

units.value: standard deviations of the within-school-year grade distribution (grades standardized to mean 0 and SD 1 within each school year)

estimand.target_population: Students who sat the class 9 nationally centralized final examination in mathematics in Denmark between 2002 and 2011 and belong to the 2.5 generation, the native-Dane group or the second generation.

population.description: All students taking the class 9 nationally centralized final examination in mathematics in Denmark, 2002-2011, classified as native Danes, 2.5 generation or second generation; children of single parents excluded.
population.selection: Students who sat the class 9 nationally centralized final examination in the subject in Denmark 2002-2011. 'Children of single parents are not included in the analysis.'

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation in parental nativity between students (and, in the fixed-effects columns, within schools or within extended families). No reform, lottery or discontinuity is used: 'the paper is mainly descriptive'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unobservable characteristics at the family level - values, upbringing practices and attitudes - are shared by intermarried and endogamously married parents and affect their children's school achievement; the author states these may bias the parameters and are not removed in this specification.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues that brothers and sisters are more likely to share these features than two random individuals and introduces cousin fixed effects to control for them partially; no test is offered.

evidence.how: The paper prints no mean of the standardized grade average for the reference group or for any student group: Tables 1 and 2 report only covariate means (parental education, birth region, separation, sex, year) and no grade means, and the table notes give none.
The outcome is standardized to SD one within each school year, so the SD of the outcome in the pooled estimation sample is 1 by construction; the paper prints no sample SD.

The paper names no register or register variable for grades or for parental country of birth: it says only that 'The analysis is based on administrative registers, covering the full population of Denmark'. The one register named anywhere is the Employment Classification Module (AKM), used for parental labour-market attachment.
The tables print standard errors in parentheses and significance stars; no confidence intervals are reported.

evidence.how: The paper prints no mean of the standardized grade average for the reference group or for any student group: Tables 1 and 2 report only covariate means (parental education, birth region, separation, sex, year) and no grade means, and the table notes give none.
The outcome is standardized to SD one within each school year, so the SD of the outcome in the pooled estimation sample is 1 by construction; the paper prints no sample SD.

The paper names no register or register variable for grades or for parental country of birth: it says only that 'The analysis is based on administrative registers, covering the full population of Denmark'. The one register named anywhere is the Employment Classification Module (AKM), used for parental labour-market attachment.
The tables print standard errors in parentheses and significance stars; no confidence intervals are reported.

claims.statement: Students classified as Native Danes differ from the 2.5 generation (children of intermarriage) in standardized class 9 mathematics grades, in the OLS with school fixed effects of Table 4, column (D) School FE.

treatment.label: Native Danes (student-group indicator; reference category: the 2.5 generation)

definition.value: Indicator for a native Dane, defined as 'Born in Denmark with both parents born in Denmark'. Estimated relative to the omitted category, the 2.5 generation, i.e. children of intermarriage born in Denmark with one native-born and one foreign-born parent.

timing.value: Parental country of birth, fixed at the child's birth; the group indicator is measured in the cross-section of the child's class 9 examination year.

outcome.label: Standardized grade average in mathematics, class 9 nationally centralized final examinations

definition.value: Grade average of the several exams taken in the subject at the nationally centralized class 9 final examination; 'grades are standardized to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one within each school year'. Cross-sectional: students take their class 9 exam once.

timing.value: Measured once, at the student's class 9 nationally centralized final examination, in the examination years 2002-2011.

units.value: standard deviations of the within-school-year grade distribution (grades standardized to mean 0 and SD 1 within each school year)

magnitude.interpretation: 'There is a very small difference between Native Danes and 1.5 generation immigrants in model D including School FE.'

estimand.target_population: Students who sat the class 9 nationally centralized final examination in mathematics in Denmark between 2002 and 2011 and belong to the 2.5 generation, the native-Dane group or the second generation.

evidence.how: The paper prints no mean of the standardized grade average for the reference group or for any student group: Tables 1 and 2 report only covariate means (parental education, birth region, separation, sex, year) and no grade means, and the table notes give none.
The outcome is standardized to SD one within each school year, so the SD of the outcome in the pooled estimation sample is 1 by construction; the paper prints no sample SD.

The paper names no register or register variable for grades or for parental country of birth: it says only that 'The analysis is based on administrative registers, covering the full population of Denmark'. The one register named anywhere is the Employment Classification Module (AKM), used for parental labour-market attachment.
The tables print standard errors in parentheses and significance stars; no confidence intervals are reported.

evidence.how: The paper prints no mean of the standardized grade average for the reference group or for any student group: Tables 1 and 2 report only covariate means (parental education, birth region, separation, sex, year) and no grade means, and the table notes give none.
The outcome is standardized to SD one within each school year, so the SD of the outcome in the pooled estimation sample is 1 by construction; the paper prints no sample SD.

The paper names no register or register variable for grades or for parental country of birth: it says only that 'The analysis is based on administrative registers, covering the full population of Denmark'. The one register named anywhere is the Employment Classification Module (AKM), used for parental labour-market attachment.
The tables print standard errors in parentheses and significance stars; no confidence intervals are reported.

evidence.how: The paper prints no mean of the standardized grade average for the reference group or for any student group: Tables 1 and 2 report only covariate means (parental education, birth region, separation, sex, year) and no grade means, and the table notes give none.
The outcome is standardized to SD one within each school year, so the SD of the outcome in the pooled estimation sample is 1 by construction; the paper prints no sample SD.

The one register named anywhere is the Employment Classification Module (AKM), used for parental labour-market attachment.
The tables print standard errors in parentheses and significance stars; no confidence intervals are reported.

evidence.how: The paper prints no mean of the standardized grade average for the reference group or for any student group: Tables 1 and 2 report only covariate means (parental education, birth region, separation, sex, year) and no grade means, and the table notes give none.
The outcome is standardized to SD one within each school year, so the SD of the outcome in the pooled estimation sample is 1 by construction; the paper prints no sample SD.

The paper names no register or register variable for grades or for parental country of birth: it says only that 'The analysis is based on administrative registers, covering the full population of Denmark'. The one register named anywhere is the Employment Classification Module (AKM), used for parental labour-market attachment.
The tables print standard errors in parentheses and significance stars; no confidence intervals are reported.

claims.statement: 2.5-generation students whose native parent is the mother (the non-native parent being the father) differ from native Danes in standardized class 9 danish grades, in the OLS with the full covariate vector panel of Table 7.

treatment.label: 2.5 generation, Mother Danish (the non-native parent is the father) (indicator; reference category: native Danes)

definition.value: Indicator for a 2.5-generation student whose native (Danish-born) parent is the mother, i.e. whose non-native parent is the father. Estimated relative to the omitted category, native Danes; second-generation immigrants are excluded from these models.

definition.value: Grade average of the several exams taken in the subject at the nationally centralized class 9 final examination; 'grades are standardized to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one within each school year'. Cross-sectional: students take their class 9 exam once.

timing.value: Measured once, at the student's class 9 nationally centralized final examination, in the examination years 2002-2011.

units.value: standard deviations of the within-school-year grade distribution (grades standardized to mean 0 and SD 1 within each school year)

magnitude.interpretation: 'Results are strikingly similar in both subjects and no differences are found between having a mother or a father that is non-native.'

key_assumptions.assumption: Unobservable characteristics at the family level - values, upbringing practices and attitudes - are shared by intermarried and endogamously married parents and affect their children's school achievement; the author states these may bias the parameters and are not removed in this specification.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues that brothers and sisters are more likely to share these features than two random individuals and introduces cousin fixed effects to control for them partially; no test is offered.

evidence.how: The paper prints no mean of the standardized grade average for the reference group or for any student group: Tables 1 and 2 report only covariate means (parental education, birth region, separation, sex, year) and no grade means, and the table notes give none.
The outcome is standardized to SD one within each school year, so the SD of the outcome in the pooled estimation sample is 1 by construction; the paper prints no sample SD.

The paper names no register or register variable for grades or for parental country of birth: it says only that 'The analysis is based on administrative registers, covering the full population of Denmark'. The one register named anywhere is the Employment Classification Module (AKM), used for parental labour-market attachment.
The tables print standard errors in parentheses and significance stars; no confidence intervals are reported.

The outcome is standardized to SD one within each school year, so the SD of the outcome in the pooled estimation sample is 1 by construction; the paper prints no sample SD.

The paper names no register or register variable for grades or for parental country of birth: it says only that 'The analysis is based on administrative registers, covering the full population of Denmark'. The one register named anywhere is the Employment Classification Module (AKM), used for parental labour-market attachment.
The tables print standard errors in parentheses and significance stars; no confidence intervals are reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unobservable characteristics at the family level - values, upbringing practices and attitudes - are shared by intermarried and endogamously married parents and affect their children's school achievement; the author states these may bias the parameters and are not removed in this specification.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues that brothers and sisters are more likely to share these features than two random individuals and introduces cousin fixed effects to control for them partially; no test is offered.

evidence.how: The paper prints no mean of the standardized grade average for the reference group or for any student group: Tables 1 and 2 report only covariate means (parental education, birth region, separation, sex, year) and no grade means, and the table notes give none.
The outcome is standardized to SD one within each school year, so the SD of the outcome in the pooled estimation sample is 1 by construction; the paper prints no sample SD.

The paper names no register or register variable for grades or for parental country of birth: it says only that 'The analysis is based on administrative registers, covering the full population of Denmark'. The one register named anywhere is the Employment Classification Module (AKM), used for parental labour-market attachment.
The tables print standard errors in parentheses and significance stars; no confidence intervals are reported.

definition.value: Indicator that the mother's highest education at the time of the child's exam is tertiary education, relative to the omitted category, primary education.

timing.value: Measured once, at the student's class 9 nationally centralized final examination, in the examination years 2002-2011.

units.value: standard deviations of the within-school-year grade distribution (grades standardized to mean 0 and SD 1 within each school year)

evidence.how: The paper prints no mean of the standardized grade average for the reference group or for any student group: Tables 1 and 2 report only covariate means (parental education, birth region, separation, sex, year) and no grade means, and the table notes give none.
The outcome is standardized to SD one within each school year, so the SD of the outcome in the pooled estimation sample is 1 by construction; the paper prints no sample SD.

The paper names no register or register variable for grades or for parental country of birth: it says only that 'The analysis is based on administrative registers, covering the full population of Denmark'. The one register named anywhere is the Employment Classification Module (AKM), used for parental labour-market attachment.
The tables print standard errors in parentheses and significance stars; no confidence intervals are reported.

definition.value: Grade average of the several exams taken in the subject at the nationally centralized class 9 final examination; 'grades are standardized to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one within each school year'. Cross-sectional: students take their class 9 exam once.

population.selection: Students who sat the class 9 nationally centralized final examination in the subject in Denmark 2002-2011. 'Children of single parents are not included in the analysis.'

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation in parental nativity between students (and, in the fixed-effects columns, within schools or within extended families). No reform, lottery or discontinuity is used: 'the paper is mainly descriptive'.

evidence.how: The paper prints no mean of the standardized grade average for the reference group or for any student group: Tables 1 and 2 report only covariate means (parental education, birth region, separation, sex, year) and no grade means, and the table notes give none.
The outcome is standardized to SD one within each school year, so the SD of the outcome in the pooled estimation sample is 1 by construction; the paper prints no sample SD.

The paper names no register or register variable for grades or for parental country of birth: it says only that 'The analysis is based on administrative registers, covering the full population of Denmark'. The one register named anywhere is the Employment Classification Module (AKM), used for parental labour-market attachment.
The tables print standard errors in parentheses and significance stars; no confidence intervals are reported.

ambiguities: Tables 3 and 4 print 'Yes' as the reference category of parental separation and a negative coefficient on 'No', while the text states that parental separation is associated with a negative grade outcome for children; the row labels in the table appear to be reversed.

evidence.how: The paper prints no mean of the standardized grade average for the reference group or for any student group: Tables 1 and 2 report only covariate means (parental education, birth region, separation, sex, year) and no grade means, and the table notes give none.
The outcome is standardized to SD one within each school year, so the SD of the outcome in the pooled estimation sample is 1 by construction; the paper prints no sample SD.

The paper names no register or register variable for grades or for parental country of birth: it says only that 'The analysis is based on administrative registers, covering the full population of Denmark'. The one register named anywhere is the Employment Classification Module (AKM), used for parental labour-market attachment.
The tables print standard errors in parentheses and significance stars; no confidence intervals are reported.

definition.value: Indicator printed in the row 'Parents separated / No', with 'Yes' printed as the reference category.

timing.value: Measured at the time of the child's class 9 examination (parental education is 'the highest education obtained for both the mother and the father at the time of the child's exam').

outcome.label: Standardized grade average in mathematics, class 9 nationally centralized final examinations

definition.value: Grade average of the several exams taken in the subject at the nationally centralized class 9 final examination; 'grades are standardized to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one within each school year'. Cross-sectional: students take their class 9 exam once.

timing.value: Measured once, at the student's class 9 nationally centralized final examination, in the examination years 2002-2011.

units.value: standard deviations of the within-school-year grade distribution (grades standardized to mean 0 and SD 1 within each school year)

estimand.target_population: Students who sat the class 9 nationally centralized final examination in mathematics in Denmark between 2002 and 2011.

population.description: All students taking the class 9 nationally centralized final examination in mathematics in Denmark, 2002-2011, classified as native Danes, 2.5 generation or second generation; children of single parents excluded.
population.selection: Students who sat the class 9 nationally centralized final examination in the subject in Denmark 2002-2011. 'Children of single parents are not included in the analysis.'

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation in parental nativity between students (and, in the fixed-effects columns, within schools or within extended families). No reform, lottery or discontinuity is used: 'the paper is mainly descriptive'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unobservable characteristics at the family level - values, upbringing practices and attitudes - are shared by intermarried and endogamously married parents and affect their children's school achievement; the author states these may bias the parameters and are not removed in this specification.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues that brothers and sisters are more likely to share these features than two random individuals and introduces cousin fixed effects to control for them partially; no test is offered.
